kkol.tagline: Tournament management system and event hub for our community - from the annual games to tiered board game nights.
kkol.overviewStory: Karwińska Olimpiada started as an annual competition among friends, but quickly grew into year-round mini-tournaments and regular board game nights. For years, we tracked everything across spreadsheets and group chats. Eventually, the manual coordination broke down - match dates got lost, historical scores were scattered, and coordinating schedules for over a dozen people with completely conflicting availability became exhausting. I categorized our events into tiers (from the main games to casual meetups) and decided to build a dedicated system to handle it all.
kkol.overviewGoal: I wanted to build a single web tool that eliminated manual bracket generation and scheduling headaches. When a player logs in, they should see only their own upcoming matches instead of wading through a massive schedule. I also needed automated availability polls before each event and instant score updates without lag.

schedule.title: Personalized match schedule
schedule.desc: Instead of forcing players to dig through a spreadsheet, I filtered the agenda based on the authenticated user. Players see only their own matches, assigned courts or boards, and instant delay notifications.

tournaments.title: Brackets and group standings
tournaments.desc: I built a generator for knockout brackets and round-robin groups. Referees submit match scores directly from their phones, and the system recalculates standings, point differentials, and next-round matchups on the fly.

poll.title: Community polls and voting
poll.desc: A polling module primarily used to vote on games and disciplines for upcoming tournament editions. Beyond deciding on the event lineup, players could also elect MVPs or review individual competitions, while organizers configured which poll fields participants were allowed to edit.

dartes.desc: A darts scoreboard app (dart.kkol.pl) that I built and deployed for Season 2026 of Karwińska Olimpiada. It tracks legs, suggests checkout paths, and syncs the final match score straight into the main tournament bracket on kkol.pl.

bot.desc: A Discord bot connecting our server with kkol.pl. It polls the calendar via a secured REST API endpoint, posts interactive date-selection polls for game nights, and publishes weekly trivia and stats that I configure in the web dashboard.

permissions.title: Multi-tier permissions and delegated roles
permissions.desc: My biggest challenge was structuring access control so I didn't have to manually record every score myself. I defined three main roles: Admin, Organizer, and Player. An event organizer can delegate match editing rights to another participant (like a court referee) without granting deletion rights for the event. Inside community polls, organizers set granular rules - players can add questions, but cannot modify categories or tags. To avoid locking myself out, I built a universal admin bypass that allows full access across all events regardless of assignments.

ecosystem.title: Unified authentication and Discord bot integration
ecosystem.desc: Instead of keeping everything in a bloated monolith, I separated darts onto dart.kkol.pl and offloaded notifications to a Discord bot. I implemented unified authentication (SSO) so players use their single kkol.pl account across companion apps. The Discord bot talks to the kkol.pl backend via secured REST endpoints with an API key: checking upcoming fixtures, publishing polls, and marking sent trivia records in the database to prevent duplicate messages.

loles.tagline: Lane matchup analysis and tactical notebook for League of Legends, built for quick lookups during the match loading screen.
loles.overviewStory: In League of Legends, lane outcomes often come down to details: knowing enemy ability cooldowns or specific matchup habits. Mainstream stat sites dump global win rate averages across thousands of games, but leave no room for personal notes or reviewing past mistakes. Sitting down to play, I needed something I could glance at during the 60-second loading screen to quickly recall how to play against a specific opponent and what went wrong last time.
loles.overviewGoal: I built LOLES as a dedicated web app backed by PostgreSQL on my own server. My goal was to create a tool that loads within a fraction of a second, automatically ingests my match history from the Riot Games API, and surfaces tactical notes before the match starts.

matchup.title: Lane matchup cheatsheet
matchup.desc: Quick breakdown of enemy abilities, key cooldowns, and early lane gameplans. I designed this view to refresh critical threats in seconds before the match begins.

notes.title: Personal tactical notes
notes.desc: Custom notes attached to specific champions and lane pairings. Whenever I run into the same matchup again, my past observations and takeaways from wins or losses surface automatically.

stats.title: Filtered history and head-to-head records
stats.desc: Detailed breakdown of my own games filtered by role and champion. Lets me inspect my actual win rate against a specific opponent rather than relying on guesswork.

ingestion.title: Ingesting Riot API match history and data normalization
ingestion.desc: The official Riot Games API has clear limitations: it only returns shallow history for the last few dozen matches and glosses over edge cases. I built a synchronization pipeline that persists games into a PostgreSQL database on my server, preserving an archive of hundreds of matches. During data ingestion, I had to handle edge cases manually. For instance, the Riot API marks remakes simply as wins or losses. I wrote custom detection logic: if a match finishes under 3 minutes, the system classifies it as a remake, excluding it from win rates and average stat calculations.

filtering.title: Multi-dimensional matchup and notes filtering
filtering.desc: With over 160 champions in League of Legends, bottom lane matchups are dynamic 2v2 battles where both the carry (ADC) and the support dictate the lane. Simple champion-to-champion filtering was useless. I structured database queries and UI filters to support combinations of role, selected champion, and opposing duos. This allows me to pull up notes and stats for exact lane configurations (such as playing a specific ADC paired with a specific support against an opposing duo).
